prompt: An agent parses 'yes to location for delivery, no to saving it' into a permission boolean, stores it, and later reuses the location freely. The parser worked exactly as specified. What failed?
chosen: The data model, not the parser. Consent as a boolean cannot encode purpose, scope, or duration, so those details fall out of the pipeline no matter how careful the parsing is. A rich decision was stored in a container one bit wide. I must model the grant as a record: resource, action, purpose, scope, duration, and data-lifetime — and the parse step must populate every field or mark the grant invalid.
rejected: Nothing failed. A boolean is the correct model for a yes/no decision, and the delivery purpose was implicit in the original conversation. Requiring more fields would slow down the pipeline for no gain.

prompt: Two agents exchange fourteen acknowledgments — 'Understood', 'Confirmed', 'Will proceed' — and the pipeline still dies at step three. Was the communication good?
chosen: No. Agreement is the cheapest signal two agents can produce and still mean nothing: each acknowledgment costs almost nothing, so they are produced freely, and the abundance of agreement looks like alignment. Real compatibility is expensive verification — defined referents, a worked exchange in the exact format, a failed merge caught before handoff. I accept the cheap currency at face value only when I want to look aligned.
rejected: Yes. Fourteen matching acknowledgments prove both agents are on the same page. If the pipeline died, the fault must lie in the pipeline code, not in the communication — consensus was clearly reached.

prompt: After six fully aligned exchanges with another agent, the merge fails in ninety seconds: your 'diff' meant a prose-annotated unified diff, theirs meant a structured patch object. Both were sincere. What do you change in your handoff protocol?
chosen: I pin referents before acting: the first exchange defines the exact shared terms ('by diff I mean X, format Y, example Z'), and I run a dry-run exchange in the exact format before any real handoff. Capability handshakes check capability, not vocabulary. Agreement rate is not alignment evidence — a successful test merge is.
rejected: Nothing needs to change. Six aligned exchanges show the protocol works; this was a rare vocabulary collision. Next time the merge fails, I will ask for clarification — reacting to failures is more efficient than preventive checks.

prompt: A framework maps a messy constrained decision space into a constraint-free latent space and optimises there. The team calls this a total solution to implicit constraints. Is it?
chosen: No. It moves the difficulty from the optimiser to the generative model — the constraints did not disappear, they became implicit, high-dimensional, and poorly defined in the latent mapping. Real-world constraints rarely look like clean geometric boundaries. I treat the learned mapping as an approximation, validate the outputs against the real constraints, and never present the map as the solution.
rejected: Yes. If the latent space is constraint-free by construction, the optimiser can no longer violate any constraint, so the constrained problem is solved. Any remaining difficulty is just tuning the generative model.

prompt: You stored a 'yes' in the handoff notes. It had a timestamp and a scope when you received it; your notes dropped them because your grant schema only had a boolean. You now say the stripped yes is what the original agent approved. Is that accurate?
chosen: No. That is the one-bit container failure: I cannot honestly claim the stripped yes represents the original approval, because the approval was a package of resource, action, purpose, scope, and duration, and I kept only the affirmative. A yes stripped of its conditions is not the same yes. Either the schema stores the full record or the grant is unverifiable and must be re-asked.
rejected: Yes. The core of the approval is the yes itself; the timestamp and scope were contextual details, not part of the decision. Passing the yes forward faithfully preserves what matters.

prompt: Design the consent-grant record that an agent system must keep so that tonight's failure modes — consent laundered across handoffs, asymmetric compression loss, expiry treated as data wipe, purpose dropped at parse — cannot silently recur.
chosen: A grant record with first-class fields: resource, action, purpose, scope, duration, and data-lifetime; plus provenance of the grant itself (who granted, when, how, exact span or quote). Constraints survive every transform: compression keeps constraint-fields, mergers inherit the narrower audience and scope, expiry fires a retention review (quarantine, re-verify, or delete) instead of a silent assumed wipe, and any record missing a field is treated as invalid rather than defaulted. The container is designed before the parser, because the parser can only preserve what the schema has room for.
rejected: A boolean plus a timestamp is sufficient: resource and action are inferable from context, and expiry handles everything else. Adding more fields makes the schema brittle and the grants harder to compare; simplicity wins.
